explanation: For a system-assigned identity you set acrUseManagedIdentityCreds to true and grant that identity AcrPull (data-plane read) on the registry. acrUserManagedIdentityID is only for user-assigned identities, and Contributor is control-plane, not the data-plane pull role. Enabling the admin account contradicts the no-admin/no-credential requirement. AcrPush grants write access it does not need, and anonymous pull defeats the keyless private-pull goal.

stem: A pod on AKS shows a container status of OOMKilled with exit code 137. Which statement accurately describes what happened?
choices: The whole pod was evicted by the kubelet because the node ran low on memory
The pod failed its readiness probe and was removed from the Service
The node was cordoned and drained during a rolling upgrade
The container exceeded its memory limit and was terminated by the kernel OOM killer, then restarted, while other containers in the pod can keep running
explanation: OOMKilled is a container-level event: the container that breaches its memory limit is killed by the Linux OOM killer (exit 137) and restarted; sibling containers can continue. Node-pressure eviction is a separate pod-level mechanism reported as Failed/Evicted, not OOMKilled. Readiness-probe failure removes the pod from Service endpoints but does not produce exit 137. Cordon/drain is an upgrade operation, not an OOM kill.

stem: A container at Woodgrove is intermittently inaccessible and its container keeps restarting with reason OOMKilled; the spec sets a memory limit of 256Mi. Which action addresses the root cause?
choices: Add a liveness probe so Kubernetes restarts the container faster
Set memory requests and limits based on the app's measured usage (raise the limit if needed)
Increase the Deployment replica count to spread the load
Add more nodes to the cluster
explanation: OOMKilled means the container needs more memory than its limit allows; measuring actual usage and setting appropriate requests/limits is the root-cause fix. A liveness probe only restarts the container faster and treats the symptom. Adding replicas or nodes does not change a single container's per-container memory limit, so each replica still gets OOMKilled.

stem: Before you can split incoming traffic between two revisions of an Azure Container App, what must you do first?
choices: Enable multiple revision mode on the container app
Create a second Container Apps environment
Deploy the revisions as separate container apps
Enable Dapr on both revisions
explanation: Traffic splitting is only available in multiple revision mode; single revision mode always routes all traffic to the latest revision. A second environment or separate apps would not be two revisions of one app. Dapr is unrelated to revision traffic weighting.

stem: An operator updates the value of a secret referenced by a running Azure Container App. Which statement is correct?
choices: The secret change automatically creates a new revision
The app must be deleted and recreated to read the new value
Secrets can only be changed by redeploying the entire environment
The change is application-scope, so no new revision is created and existing revisions must be restarted or a new revision deployed to pick up the value
explanation: Secrets are application-scope; changing them does not create a new revision, and existing revisions must be restarted (or a new revision deployed) to see the updated value. Secret changes do not trigger a new revision automatically. Deleting the app or redeploying the environment is unnecessary and far beyond what is required.

stem: Relecloud wants a Container App to scale to zero when idle but keep at least two replicas when busy. Which scale-rule type prevents scaling to zero and must therefore be avoided as the only trigger if scale-to-zero is required?
choices: Azure Service Bus queue length rule
HTTP concurrent-requests rule
CPU or memory utilization rule
Cron/scheduled rule
explanation: Apps that scale on CPU or memory load cannot scale to zero, so a CPU/memory rule as the sole trigger blocks scale-to-zero. Queue-length, HTTP, and scheduled KEDA rules all support scaling to zero; only resource (CPU/memory) rules keep at least one replica running.

stem: Litware wants to run a GPU-accelerated inference Container App using serverless (Consumption) GPU that scales to zero. Which environment prerequisite must be satisfied?
choices: A Consumption-only environment is sufficient
The app must run in a workload profiles environment; Consumption-only environments do not support GPU
GPU is available only on Azure Container Instances, not Container Apps
A Dedicated GPU profile must be added after the app is created
explanation: Serverless GPUs require a workload profiles environment; Consumption-only environments do not support GPU. A Consumption-only environment cannot host GPU. Container Apps does support serverless GPU (not only ACI). Dedicated GPU profiles must be configured when the environment is created, not added afterward, and are separate from serverless Consumption GPU.

stem: A nightly batch process at Proseware must run on a fixed cron schedule, execute to completion, and then stop. Which Azure Container Apps job trigger type fits best?
choices: Manual
Event
Schedule
Ingress
explanation: A Schedule-triggered job runs on a cron expression, executes to completion, and stops, matching a nightly batch. Manual runs only on demand (a single execution you start). Event triggers scale on an event source, not a fixed clock. Ingress is not a job trigger type.

stem: An event-driven Container Apps job at Adventure Works must process a batch where up to 10 replicas run at once and the job is considered complete only after 200 replicas finish successfully. Which two properties encode this?
choices: parallelism = 200 and replicaCompletionCount = 10
parallelism = 10 and replicaCompletionCount = 200
maxSurge = 10 and maxUnavailable = 200
minReplicas = 10 and maxReplicas = 200
explanation: parallelism caps concurrent replicas (10) and replicaCompletionCount sets the number of successful completions required for overall completion (200). Swapping the values would run 200 at once and finish after 10, the opposite of the requirement. maxSurge/maxUnavailable are Kubernetes rolling-update fields, and minReplicas/maxReplicas are app scaling settings, not job completion controls.

stem: Fourth Coffee wants application images to rebuild automatically whenever the shared base image is patched and pushed to the registry, with no manual step. Which ACR Tasks capability provides this?
choices: A quick task run with az acr build
A multi-step task run manually with az acr run
A retention policy on the registry
A base image update trigger on an automatically triggered task
explanation: An automatically triggered task with a base image update trigger detects the new base image and rebuilds dependent application images automatically. A quick task and a manually run multi-step task both require you to invoke them. A retention policy manages image cleanup, not rebuilds.

stem: Graphic Design Institute uses ACR Tasks with a Git repository context. Which trigger is enabled by default?
choices: Pull request trigger
Commit trigger
Timer/scheduled trigger
Base image update trigger for public Docker Hub bases
explanation: For a Git context, the commit trigger is enabled by default; a code commit starts a build. Pull-request triggers are not enabled by default. Timer and base-image triggers must be configured explicitly and are not the default Git trigger.

stem: Which statement about the az acr build command is correct?
choices: It builds the image in the cloud close to the registry and pushes it to the registry on success, without requiring a local Docker install
It builds the image on your local Docker daemon and then uploads it
It only validates the Dockerfile syntax without producing an image
It requires the registry admin account to be enabled
explanation: az acr build performs a quick task that builds natively in Azure and pushes the successful image to the registry, needing no local Docker engine. It does not use the local Docker daemon, does more than syntax validation, and authenticates via Azure CLI rather than requiring the admin account.

stem: Best For You Organics must copy an image from Docker Hub into a private ACR from a management workstation that has no Docker engine installed and cannot run a build. Which command accomplishes this?
choices: docker pull then docker push
az acr build
az acr import
az acr task create
explanation: az acr import copies images between registries (including Docker Hub) directly, with no local Docker engine and no build step. docker pull/push requires a Docker engine. az acr build runs a build from a Dockerfile rather than copying an existing image. az acr task create defines an ongoing task, not a one-time import.

stem: In an App Service Linux custom container with sidecar support, which container receives inbound external traffic?
choices: Every container in the app receives external traffic
The container with the lowest target port
All sidecar containers, but not the main container
Only the container with isMain set to true
explanation: Only the main container (isMain = true) receives external traffic; sidecars have isMain = false. Sidecars do not receive external traffic, port number does not determine the main container, and the inverse (sidecars only) is wrong.

stem: A Deployment at Trey Research has 4 replicas and must stay serving during updates: at least 3 pods available at all times and extra pods allowed temporarily. Which rolling-update settings meet both constraints?
choices: maxUnavailable = 1 and maxSurge = 1
maxUnavailable = 2 and maxSurge = 0
maxUnavailable = 0 and maxSurge = 0
strategy type Recreate
explanation: maxUnavailable = 1 keeps at least 3 of 4 available, and maxSurge = 1 permits a temporary extra pod so the update proceeds smoothly. maxUnavailable = 2 would drop to 2 available, breaking the at-least-3 rule. maxUnavailable = 0 with maxSurge = 0 makes progress impossible. Recreate terminates all old pods first, causing downtime.

stem: Which statement about the maxUnavailable setting during AKS node pool upgrades is correct?
choices: It can be set on any node pool, including system node pools
It cannot be set on system node pools
It always creates surge nodes before draining
It is ignored unless Dapr is enabled
explanation: maxUnavailable cannot be set on AKS system node pools; it applies to user node pools for in-place, cordon-and-drain upgrades. It is specifically disallowed on system node pools. Unlike max surge, maxUnavailable does not create surge nodes; it cordons and drains in place. Dapr is unrelated to node upgrades.

stem: VanArsdel must dedicate a GPU node pool so that only GPU workloads run there AND those GPU pods run nowhere else. Which combination achieves both directions of isolation?
choices: A nodeSelector on the pods only
A NoSchedule taint on the nodes only
A NoSchedule taint plus matching toleration, and a nodeSelector or node affinity on the pods for the GPU node label
A PreferNoSchedule taint on the nodes only
explanation: The taint plus toleration keeps non-GPU pods off the GPU nodes; the nodeSelector/affinity forces GPU pods onto the labeled GPU nodes, covering both directions. A nodeSelector alone still lets other pods land on GPU nodes because it does not repel them. A taint alone repels others but does not force GPU pods onto those nodes. PreferNoSchedule is only a soft preference, so it does not guarantee isolation.

stem: On AKS, how does a nodeSelector differ from a node taint?
choices: A nodeSelector repels non-matching pods; a taint attracts matching pods
They are identical and interchangeable
A nodeSelector works only with spot node pools
A nodeSelector prioritizes matching nodes but does not repel other pods, whereas a taint prevents non-tolerating pods from scheduling
explanation: Pods without a matching nodeSelector can still be scheduled on labeled nodes (soft steering), while a taint hard-blocks pods that lack a matching toleration. The first option reverses their behaviors. They are not identical, and nodeSelector is not restricted to spot node pools.

stem: To schedule a pod onto an AKS Spot node pool, which pod configuration is required to match the default Spot taint kubernetes.azure.com/scalesetpriority=spot:NoSchedule?
choices: Only a higher pod priority class
A toleration for the spot taint (typically with node affinity for the spot label)
A larger memory request
An init container that removes the taint
explanation: The Spot node pool is tainted NoSchedule, so the pod needs a matching toleration (commonly paired with node affinity for the spot label) to land there. Priority class and larger memory requests do not satisfy a taint. Pods cannot remove node taints via an init container.

stem: Margie's Travel is migrating an existing Windows web application into a container and needs deployment slots for staged swaps, built-in custom domain and managed TLS, and minimal operations overhead. Which host is the best fit?
choices: Azure Kubernetes Service
Azure Container Apps
Azure App Service for Containers
Azure Container Instances
explanation: App Service offers deployment slots, built-in custom domains and managed certificates, and low operational overhead for a web app. AKS is operations-heavy and has no built-in slots. Container Apps uses revisions and traffic splitting rather than slots and lacks the same integrated TLS/domain web workflow. Container Instances has no slots, autoscaling, or managed TLS story.

stem: Which statement about enabling Dapr on an Azure Container App is correct?
choices: Dapr settings are a revision-scope change and create a new revision
Dapr settings are an application-scope change and do not create a new revision
Dapr can only be enabled by recreating the environment
Dapr requires the Dedicated plan
explanation: Dapr configuration lives in the application-scope (configuration) section, so changing it does not create a new revision. It is not revision-scope, does not require recreating the environment, and does not require the Dedicated plan.

stem: A KEDA scale rule on a Container App must authenticate to a Service Bus queue using a connection string that cannot be stored in plain text in the template. What is the recommended approach?
choices: Hard-code the connection string in the scale rule metadata
Store it in a Kubernetes ConfigMap
Pass it as a command-line argument to the container
Reference an application secret from the scale rule authentication (secretRef)
explanation: Container Apps secrets are application-scope and can be referenced from scale-rule authentication (secretRef), keeping the value out of plaintext template fields. Hard-coding or passing as an argument exposes the secret. Container Apps does not expose Kubernetes ConfigMaps to the user for this purpose.

stem: For a Deployment that must update with zero downtime, which strategy type should you choose over Recreate?
choices: RollingUpdate
Recreate
Canary (a built-in strategy type)
OnDelete
explanation: RollingUpdate incrementally replaces pods so the app stays available; Recreate terminates all old pods first, causing downtime. Recreate causes downtime. Canary and Blue are deployment patterns, not built-in Deployment strategy type values. OnDelete is a DaemonSet/StatefulSet update strategy, not a Deployment strategy type.

stem: Which Azure Container Registry tier is required to use Private Link with private endpoints?
choices: Basic
Standard
Premium
Any tier with the networking add-on
explanation: Private endpoints/Private Link for ACR is a Premium-tier capability. Basic and Standard do not support private endpoints, and there is no separate networking add-on that unlocks them below Premium.

stem: Coho Vineyard needs GPU-accelerated AI inference that scales to zero when idle, bills per second, and requires no Kubernetes cluster to manage. Which option best fits?
choices: An AKS GPU node pool
Azure Container Apps with a serverless (Consumption) GPU workload profile
An App Service Premium plan with a GPU
Azure Container Instances with a GPU SKU (generally available)
explanation: Container Apps serverless GPU provides scale-to-zero, per-second billing, and no cluster management for GPU inference. An AKS GPU node pool requires cluster management and does not natively scale GPU nodes to zero per-second. App Service does not offer GPU compute. ACI GPU SKUs are not the managed scale-to-zero, per-second serverless GPU experience described.

stem: Which characteristic accurately describes Azure Container Registry geo-replication?
choices: It uses an active-active model with eventual consistency, so any geo-replica accepts pushes, pulls, and deletes
It uses a primary-secondary model where only the home region accepts writes
Each geo-replica requires its own separate credentials and image reference
Geo-replicas are strongly consistent, so a cross-region pull immediately after a push always succeeds
explanation: ACR geo-replication is active-active with eventual consistency; every replica is writable and content syncs in the background. It is not primary-secondary. Replicas share one credential set and one global endpoint. Consistency is eventual, so a cross-region pull immediately after a push can fail with manifest unknown until replication catches up.

stem:
Complete the Azure CLI command that runs an ACR quick task to build an image in the cloud and push it to the registry on success.

```
az acr ________ \
  --registry $ACR_NAME \
  --image webapp:v1 \
  --file Dockerfile .
```
choices: run
build
task
import
explanation: az acr build performs a quick task that builds the image in Azure and pushes it to the registry when the build succeeds. az acr run executes a YAML multi-step task, not a single Dockerfile build+push. az acr task defines or manages a persistent task. az acr import copies an existing image and does not build from a Dockerfile.

stem:
Complete the kubectl command that performs a rolling update by changing the container image of a running Deployment.

```
kubectl ________ deployment/web \
  web=myregistry.azurecr.io/web:v2
```
choices: apply image
set image
patch image
edit image
explanation: kubectl set image updates the container image of a Deployment and triggers a rolling update. There is no kubectl apply image, patch image, or edit image subcommand; apply takes a manifest file, patch takes a patch document, and edit opens an editor.

stem:
Complete the kubectl command that shows the events and container statuses (including an OOMKilled reason) for a specific pod.

```
kubectl ________ pod mypod -n prod
```
choices: get
logs
describe
top
explanation: kubectl describe pod shows the Events and Container Statuses sections where the OOMKilled reason and exit code appear. kubectl get lists pods without the detailed reason. kubectl logs shows container output, not termination reason. kubectl top shows resource usage metrics, not the OOMKilled event.

stem:
Complete the Azure CLI command that assigns 80 percent of traffic to one Container Apps revision and 20 percent to another.

```
az containerapp ingress traffic ________ \
  --name orders --resource-group rg \
  --revision-weight rev-a=80 rev-b=20
```
choices: update
split
set
route
explanation: az containerapp ingress traffic set configures the per-revision traffic weights. split, update, and route are not valid subcommands of az containerapp ingress traffic; the weighting verb is set.

stem:
Complete the Azure CLI command that copies an image from Docker Hub into a private Azure Container Registry without a local Docker engine.

```
az acr ________ \
  --name myregistry \
  --source docker.io/library/nginx:latest \
  --image nginx:latest
```
choices: copy
pull
import
load
explanation: az acr import copies an image from another registry (including Docker Hub) directly into ACR, no Docker engine required. az acr copy, az acr pull, and az acr load are not valid ACR commands for this operation; import is the correct verb.

stem:
Complete the Azure CLI command that creates an AKS node pool tainted so only tolerating pods (for example GPU workloads) can schedule on it.

```
az aks nodepool add \
  --resource-group rg --cluster-name aks \
  --name gpunp \
  --________ sku=gpu:NoSchedule
```
choices: labels
node-taints
annotations
node-labels
explanation: --node-taints applies the taint (key=value:effect) to every node in the new node pool so only pods with a matching toleration schedule there. --labels and --node-labels add metadata used by nodeSelector but do not repel pods. --annotations is not a scheduling-restriction parameter.

stem: Northwind wants an App Service web app to pull a private ACR image using its already-enabled system-assigned managed identity, with no admin account and no stored registry credentials. Which two actions are required? (Select two.)
choices: Assign the AcrPull role to the web app's identity scoped to the registry
Set acrUseManagedIdentityCreds to true on the web app
Enable the ACR admin account and store the password as an app setting
Assign the Contributor role to the web app on the registry
Set acrUserManagedIdentityID to the system identity's client ID
explanation: AcrPull grants the identity data-plane pull rights, and acrUseManagedIdentityCreds = true tells App Service to authenticate to ACR with that managed identity. Enabling the admin account and storing a password contradicts the keyless requirement. Contributor is a broad control-plane role, not the pull role. acrUserManagedIdentityID applies only to user-assigned identities, not the system-assigned identity in this scenario.

stem: Which two Azure Container Registry capabilities require the Premium service tier? (Select two.)
choices: Geo-replication
Private endpoints (Private Link)
Webhook integration
Authentication with Microsoft Entra ID
The registry admin account
explanation: Geo-replication and private endpoints are Premium-only ACR features. Webhook integration, Microsoft Entra authentication, and the admin account are available on Basic and Standard tiers, so they do not require Premium.

stem: Microsoft Defender for Cloud scans images in an Azure Container Registry. Which two of the following are documented scan triggers? (Select two.)
choices: On push to the registry
On import into the registry
On deletion of a tag
On creation of the registry
On geo-replica synchronization
explanation: Defender scans images on push and on import (in addition to periodic rescans of recently pulled images). Tag deletion, registry creation, and geo-replica sync are not documented scan triggers; scanning is tied to images entering the registry, not to deletes or replication events.

stem: Which two changes to an Azure Container App are application-scope and therefore do NOT create a new revision? (Select two.)
choices: Updating a secret value
Changing traffic-splitting rules
Changing the container image
Adding a scale rule
Changing the revision suffix
explanation: Secret values and traffic-splitting rules live in the configuration (application-scope) section, so changing them does not create a new revision. Changing the container image, adding a scale rule, and changing the revision suffix are all template (revision-scope) changes that create a new revision.

stem: Wide World Importers must ensure GPU pods land only on GPU nodes and that non-GPU pods never occupy those expensive nodes. Which two measures together enforce this? (Select two.)
choices: Apply a NoSchedule taint to the GPU node pool and add a matching toleration to the GPU pods
Add a nodeSelector or node affinity for the GPU node label to the GPU pods
Increase the Deployment replica count for the GPU workload
Set maxUnavailable to 0 on the GPU node pool
Apply only a PreferNoSchedule taint to the GPU nodes
explanation: The NoSchedule taint plus toleration keeps non-GPU pods off the GPU nodes, and the nodeSelector/affinity forces GPU pods onto the labeled GPU nodes. Raising replica count does not control placement. maxUnavailable affects upgrades, not scheduling. PreferNoSchedule is only a soft preference and does not guarantee non-GPU pods stay off.

stem: Contoso maintains a base image and an application image in the same Premium registry. An ACR task must rebuild the application image automatically whenever the base image is patched. The task was created but never runs on a base-image push. Which condition must be satisfied for the base-image update trigger to fire?
choices: The base image must be re-tagged with a new unique version tag on each patch so the trigger can compare digests
The application image must be a buildtime stage in a multi-stage Dockerfile so ACR can track it as an intermediate image
The task must be run at least once so ACR can determine and track the application image dependencies, and the base image must carry a stable tag
The base-image-trigger-enabled property must be explicitly set to False so ACR switches to dependency polling
explanation: ACR only tracks dependencies after the task builds the image at least once, and it triggers only when the base image uses a stable tag such as node:9-alpine. A new unique version tag does NOT trigger a rebuild; only stable-tag updates do. base-image-trigger-enabled is True by default and setting it False disables the trigger. ACR tracks base images for runtime (application) images, not intermediate buildtime stages in multi-stage Dockerfiles.

stem: Fabrikam converts a registry to RBAC Registry + ABAC Repository Permissions mode. A service principal that previously held AcrPush now fails to push images. The team wants the principal to push to every repository, exactly as before. Which action restores registry-wide push access?
choices: Assign the Container Registry Repository Writer role without any ABAC conditions
Assign the Owner role, which grants data plane push permissions in ABAC-enabled registries
Assign the Container Registry Repository Writer role with an ABAC condition matching a repository wildcard prefix
Reassign the legacy AcrPush role, which is honored again once ABAC conditions are added
explanation: An ABAC-enabled role assigned without conditions acts as a registry-wide assignment, equivalent to the legacy AcrPush role. A wildcard-prefix condition scopes the assignment to matching repositories only, not registry-wide. Legacy AcrPush is not honored in ABAC-enabled registries regardless of conditions. Owner in an ABAC-enabled registry grants only control plane permissions, not data plane push.

stem: Tailwind Traders grants a monitoring identity the Container Registry Repository Reader role scoped with an ABAC condition to the payments repository. The identity can pull from payments but the vulnerability scanner cannot enumerate the registry catalog to discover other repositories. Which additional role assignment is required, and how must it be scoped?
choices: Assign Container Registry Repository Catalog Lister, which cannot take ABAC conditions and therefore lists all repositories
Assign the Reader control plane role scoped to the registry to enable catalog enumeration
Assign Container Registry Repository Contributor scoped to payments to inherit catalog listing
Add a second ABAC condition to the Repository Reader assignment granting the _catalog action
explanation: Repository Reader does not grant catalog listing; the separate Catalog Lister role does, and it does not support ABAC conditions so it always lists all repositories. ABAC conditions cannot add catalog list permission to Repository Reader. Repository Contributor also lacks catalog list permission. The control plane Reader role does not grant data plane catalog enumeration.

stem: Adventure Works must give a fleet of IoT devices individual, time-limited pull access to a single repository, without creating Microsoft Entra identities for each device. Which authentication mechanism meets all three constraints?
choices: The registry admin account shared across all devices
Non-Microsoft Entra repository-scoped tokens paired with a scope map
Container Registry Repository Reader role assignments with ABAC repository conditions
AKS cross-tenant service principal role assignments
explanation: Non-Entra tokens with scope maps provide scoped, time-limited repository access without requiring a Microsoft Entra identity per device. ABAC role assignments require Microsoft Entra identities, which the scenario forbids. The single admin account is registry-wide and not per-device. Cross-tenant service principals are Entra-based and not per-device scoped.

stem: Northwind configures ACR-to-ACR artifact caching so a downstream Premium registry mirrors a repository from an upstream registry. Pulls succeed but the team must avoid storing any username or password in Azure Key Vault. Which configuration satisfies the no-stored-credentials constraint while still authenticating to the upstream registry?
choices: Authenticate with a user-assigned managed identity granted Container Registry Repository Reader on the ABAC-enabled upstream registry, referenced by the cache rule --identity parameter
Enable anonymous pull on the upstream registry and create the cache rule with no credentials
Create a credential set in Key Vault holding the upstream admin username and password, referenced by -c on the cache rule
Use a non-Entra repository-scoped token from the upstream registry stored as a Key Vault secret
explanation: ACR-to-ACR caching authenticates with a user-assigned managed identity holding Repository Reader on the ABAC-enabled upstream registry, so no credentials are stored in Key Vault. A credential set stores the username and password in Key Vault, which is forbidden. Anonymous pull is not the azurecr.io upstream path and weakens security. A token stored as a Key Vault secret still stores a credential.

stem: Woodgrove Bank sources images from Docker Hub through an ACR artifact cache rule to avoid Docker Hub rate limits. Anonymous pulls of these public images previously worked directly. What is required to create the Docker Hub cache rule?
choices: Nothing extra, because Docker Hub cache rules are created without credentials like Microsoft Artifact Registry
The Basic tier is insufficient; artifact cache requires the Premium tier for Docker Hub
A connected registry in ReadOnly mode acting as the Docker Hub proxy
A credential set, because Docker Hub as an artifact cache upstream supports authenticated pulls only
explanation: As an artifact cache upstream, Docker Hub supports authenticated pulls only, so a credential set is required to create the cache rule. Unlike Microsoft Artifact Registry which supports unauthenticated pulls, Docker Hub requires credentials. A connected registry is a separate on-premises feature, not a Docker Hub proxy. Artifact cache is available in Basic, Standard, and Premium tiers, not Premium only.

stem: Relecloud deploys a connected registry on an Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes cluster. The parent cloud registry is in ReadOnly mode. The on-premises team wants the connected registry in ReadWrite mode so developers can push locally and sync up to the cloud. Why does creation of the ReadWrite child fail?
choices: ReadWrite mode is only valid when the connected registry is deployed on an IoT Edge device, not on Arc-enabled Kubernetes
A connected registry must be compatible with its parent; if the parent uses ReadOnly mode, the child must also use ReadOnly
ReadWrite requires the parent registry to be geo-replicated to at least two regions first
The child inherits the parent mode automatically, so the explicit --mode ReadWrite flag is rejected as redundant
explanation: If the parent registry uses ReadOnly mode, child registries must also use ReadOnly; only a ReadWrite parent allows either mode in children. Deployment target (Arc-enabled Kubernetes vs IoT Edge) does not govern the mode. Geo-replication is unrelated to connected registry mode compatibility. The mode is not silently inherited; the constraint is a compatibility rule with the parent, not a redundancy rejection.

stem: Proseware runs a CI pipeline that pushes myapp:v1 to the East US geo-replica of a Premium registry, then AKS pods in West Europe immediately pull myapp:v1 and intermittently fail with manifest unknown. Given ACR geo-replication uses an active-active model with eventual consistency, which mitigation directly addresses the failure?
choices: Move ACR Tasks to the West Europe region so the push originates closer to the consumers
Disable eventual consistency on the registry so all geo-replicas update synchronously
Switch the registry to a primary-secondary replication model so only East US accepts writes
Have pods pull from the West Europe regional endpoint after a webhook confirms replication completed in that geo-replica, or add retry with backoff
explanation: Eventual consistency means a cross-region pull can race replication; using webhooks to confirm replication or adding retry with backoff resolves the manifest unknown failures. ACR geo-replication is always active-active; there is no primary-secondary option to select. Synchronous consistency cannot be enabled; the model is eventual by design. ACR Tasks are bound to the home region and cannot be relocated to a replica; this does not fix cross-region replication lag.

stem: VanArsdel enables regional endpoints on a geo-replicated Premium registry and pins East US AKS clusters to myregistry.eastus.geo.azurecr.io for predictable routing. During an East US regional degradation, those clusters stop pulling and are not rerouted. Why?
choices: Regional endpoints are Basic-tier only and lack the failover logic present in Premium
Health-aware failover applies only to the global endpoint; a regional endpoint talks directly to one geo-replica and is not automatically rerouted
The home region must be East US for regional-endpoint failover to activate
Regional endpoints require dedicated data endpoints, and without them failover is disabled
explanation: Health-aware failover reroutes only global endpoint traffic; when you pin to a regional endpoint you target one geo-replica directly and ACR does not auto-reroute if that region degrades. Dedicated data endpoints affect layer blob download paths, not failover eligibility. The home region does not govern regional-endpoint failover. Regional endpoints are a Premium-tier feature, not Basic; the tier is not the cause.

stem: Litware disables public network access on a Premium registry and adds a private endpoint. Microsoft Defender for Cloud vulnerability scanning of pushed images stops producing findings. Which single setting restores scanning while keeping public access disabled?
choices: Re-enable public network access temporarily during each daily rescan window
Assign the Defender scanner the AcrQuarantineReader role on the registry
Enable the network setting that allows trusted Microsoft services to access the registry
Switch the registry to RBAC Registry + ABAC Repository Permissions mode
explanation: When network rules restrict a registry, enabling allow trusted Microsoft services lets Defender for Cloud authenticate and pull images to scan them. Re-enabling public access defeats the requirement to keep it disabled. AcrQuarantineReader governs quarantined images, not Defender network access. The role assignment permission mode does not control network access for the scanner.

stem: Munson's Pickles pushes an image to a registry monitored by Microsoft Defender for Containers, remediates a critical finding, and pushes the fixed image with the same tag. Later, Defender still reports the old vulnerability. Given how Defender scans registry images, what is the most likely explanation?
choices: The old image still exists in the registry and can be pulled by its digest, so its findings persist until it is removed
Defender only scans images on the first push and never rescans after remediation
Retagging an image prevents Defender from scanning it entirely
Findings for the old image are removed within one hour of any new push to the registry
explanation: Reassigning a tag leaves the old image resolvable by digest; if it has findings and can still be pulled, Defender continues to surface those vulnerabilities. Defender performs daily rescans of images pushed or pulled in the last 30 days, so it does rescan. Retagging does not block scanning. Finding removal is tied to image deletion, not to a new push of a different image.

stem: Coho Vineyard implements the Quarantine pattern for third-party OCI artifacts. The orchestrator imports an external image into an untrusted quarantine registry, runs CVE and malware checks, and only then promotes it. Which statement about the quarantine registry's role is correct?
choices: It holds a local copy of the image so validations run against tampering-resistant, workload-isolated content before promotion to the trusted registry
It is the same registry as the trusted store, distinguished only by a repository namespace
It replaces the need for Microsoft Defender for Containers scanning on the trusted registry
It rewrites the image layers to strip detected vulnerabilities before promotion
explanation: The quarantine registry imports a local copy that is isolated from workloads during validation, protecting against tampering and consumption until the image is deemed trusted. The quarantine process does not change the artifact composition; it validates, it does not remediate layers. Quarantine and trusted stores are segmented, not the same registry with a namespace. Defender continues to cover all registries; quarantine does not replace it.

stem: Fourth Coffee runs a custom Linux container in Azure App Service. The container listens on port 8080, but App Service returns HTTP errors because it forwards requests to the default port. The team wants the fewest changes. Which single configuration resolves this?
choices: Set WEBSITE_SWAP_WARMUP_PING_PATH to the port number
Enable the sidecar feature and route port 8080 through a proxy sidecar
Set the WEBSITES_PORT app setting to 8080
Expose two ports in the Dockerfile so App Service can negotiate the correct one
explanation: App Service assumes port 80 by default; setting WEBSITES_PORT to the container's listening port tells App Service where to forward HTTP requests. App Service allows a container to expose only one port for HTTP; adding a second does not help. WEBSITE_SWAP_WARMUP_PING_PATH configures slot-swap warm-up, not the container port. A proxy sidecar is unnecessary complexity when WEBSITES_PORT solves it directly.

stem: Alpine Ski House wants its App Service custom container to pull its image from Azure Container Registry without any stored registry credentials, using a user-assigned managed identity. Which two-part configuration is required?
choices: Enable the system-assigned identity only, because user-assigned identities cannot pull from ACR
Grant the identity Owner on the registry and set WEBSITES_PORT to the registry login server
Grant the identity AcrPull on the registry, set acrUseManagedIdentityCreds to true, and set acrUserManagedIdentityID to the identity client ID
Store the registry admin credentials as slot settings and mark them sticky
explanation: The app needs AcrPull on the registry, acrUseManagedIdentityCreds set to true, and for a user-assigned identity, acrUserManagedIdentityID set to that identity's client ID. Owner is excessive and WEBSITES_PORT is unrelated to registry auth. User-assigned identities are explicitly supported for ACR pull. Storing admin credentials contradicts the credential-free requirement.

stem: Trey Research enables a sidecar-enabled Linux custom container app in App Service with an nginx main container and an OpenTelemetry collector sidecar. External HTTP traffic must reach only nginx. How is this guaranteed in the sitecontainers configuration?
choices: Only the container with the highest target-port receives external traffic
Each sidecar sets a WEBSITES_PORT value lower than the main container's port
The collector sidecar is deployed to a separate deployment slot from the main container
The main container is marked isMain true and receives external traffic; every sidecar is marked isMain false
explanation: In a sidecar-enabled Linux app, only the container with isMain set to true receives external traffic; all sidecars set isMain to false. WEBSITES_PORT ordering does not determine which container is public. Sidecars share the app, not separate slots. Target-port magnitude does not select the public container; the isMain flag does.

stem: Best For You Organics runs a production App Service app in the Standard tier and wants zero-downtime deploys with pre-swap validation on a staging slot. During a swap, which behavior is correct regarding where initialization occurs?
choices: Initialization of the swapped app happens on the source slot while the target production slot stays online, so no requests are dropped
Initialization happens on the target slot, which briefly goes offline until warm-up completes
The source slot is deleted after the swap and recreated from the target
Both slots go offline simultaneously during the routing switch
explanation: All initialization work happens on the source slot; the target slot remains online while the source is prepared and warmed up, so traffic redirection is seamless. The target slot does not go offline; that is the point of slot swaps. Both slots are never offline together. The source slot is not deleted; it receives the previous production app after the swap.

stem: Graphic Design Institute needs a connection string and a database region setting to stay with the production slot and never move during a swap, while application build settings should swap normally. Which mechanism achieves the connection-string requirement?
choices: Move the connection string into the Dockerfile so it is baked into the image
Rely on the default, because connection strings are always slot specific and never swap
Set WEBSITE_OVERRIDE_STICKY_EXTENSION_VERSIONS to 0 on both slots
Mark the connection string as a deployment slot setting so it becomes sticky and does not swap
explanation: Connection strings swap by default but can be configured to stick to a slot by marking them as deployment slot settings. Connection strings are NOT slot specific by default; they swap unless marked sticky. WEBSITE_OVERRIDE_STICKY_EXTENSION_VERSIONS governs site extension versions, not connection strings. Baking secrets into the image is a poor practice and removes runtime configurability.

stem: Margie's Travel runs Web App for Containers on Linux and wants every push of a new image to a staging slot to trigger an automatic swap into production once warmed up. The team finds the feature unavailable. Why?
choices: Auto swap is disabled whenever a health check path is configured
Auto swap is not supported in web apps on Linux and in Web App for Containers
Auto swap requires the Isolated tier, which the plan does not use
Auto swap requires WEBSITES_PORT to be unset on the staging slot
explanation: Auto swap is explicitly not supported for web apps on Linux and for Web App for Containers. Auto swap works on Standard and higher tiers, not only Isolated. A configured health check path does not disable auto swap. WEBSITES_PORT is unrelated to auto swap availability.

stem: Woodgrove enables swap-with-preview to validate a staging slot before completing a swap into production, but the portal rejects the preview action. The team recently enabled App Service authentication on the production slot. What is the cause?
choices: Swap with preview requires a warm-up ping path returning status 200 only
Swap with preview cannot be used when site authentication is enabled in one of the slots
Swap with preview requires the source and target to be in different App Service plans
Swap with preview is only available on Windows plans, and the app runs on Linux
explanation: Swap with preview is not available when site authentication is enabled in one of the slots. Swap requires slots in the same plan, not different plans. Swap with preview is not restricted to Windows. Warm-up ping status configuration does not block preview; enabled authentication does.

stem: Litware configures App Service Health check with a status path. The team wants unhealthy instances automatically removed and replaced. On which plan does automatic replacement actually occur, and what is the aggregation behavior?
choices: Free or Shared tier; a single failed ping immediately replaces the instance
Only Isolated tier; the threshold aggregation is disabled so failures show instantly
Any tier; replacement occurs on the first failed ping regardless of scale-out
Basic tier or higher with scale-out to two or more instances; the metric deems an instance unhealthy only after consecutive failed pings reach the configured threshold
explanation: Health check needs Basic or higher with two or more instances to replace unhealthy instances; an instance is deemed unhealthy only after consecutive failed pings reach the threshold, which defaults to 10 minutes. Free and Shared plans cannot scale out, so unhealthy instances are not automatically replaced there. Replacement is not first-ping and not on any tier. Isolated is not the only qualifying tier, and threshold aggregation is not disabled.

stem: Fabrikam configures Azure Monitor autoscale on an App Service plan with two scale-out rules on CPU and HTTP queue length, plus two matching scale-in rules. During a spike, only one metric crosses its threshold. What does autoscale do?
choices: Scales in, because unmet rules default to scale-in
Scales out only after both metrics cross their thresholds in the same evaluation
Scales out, because autoscale scales out if any rule is met
Does nothing, because scale-out requires all rules to be met
explanation: Autoscale scales out if any of the rules are met (OR logic) and scales in only if all rules are met (AND logic). Scale-out uses OR logic, so one rule is sufficient; it does not require all rules. Unmet rules do not trigger scale-in. Both metrics crossing is not required for scale-out.

stem: Adventure Works sets up an autoscale scale-out rule to add an instance when sessions per instance exceed 70, sourced from an Application Insights metric. The rule fires far too early because it uses the total session count across all instances. Which setting fixes the per-instance calculation?
choices: Set the default instance count higher so the average is diluted
Lower the scale-out threshold to 70 divided by the maximum instance count
Change the metric source from Application Insights to the App Service plan
Enable the metric divide by instance count option so the threshold is evaluated per instance
explanation: Enabling metric divide by instance count evaluates the metric per instance, so sessions per instance is measured against the threshold. Manually dividing the threshold is fragile and does not track instance count changes. Changing the metric source does not by itself compute per-instance values. The default instance count is a safety fallback, not a per-instance divisor.

stem: Northwind uses non-Entra tokens and scope maps for repository access and separately wants a service principal to have write access to only two repositories. Which statement about combining these approaches is correct?
choices: Repository-scoped permissions from tokens cannot be assigned to a Microsoft Entra identity; use ABAC conditions on Container Registry Repository Writer for the service principal
A service principal must use the admin account password to inherit scope map permissions
Tokens and ABAC conditions are mutually exclusive and cannot both exist on one registry
Scope maps can be attached directly to the service principal to grant the two-repository write access
explanation: Tokens and scope maps cannot be assigned to Microsoft Entra identities; to scope a service principal to specific repositories, use ABAC conditions on an ABAC-enabled role such as Repository Writer. Scope maps bind to tokens, not directly to Entra service principals. Tokens and ABAC can coexist on a registry. The admin account is a shared registry-wide credential, not a scope map inheritance path.

stem: Proseware runs an ACR multi-step task defined in YAML that must build an image, run it in a temporary container to execute integration tests, and push it only if the tests succeed. Which task step type runs the arbitrary container command for the test phase?
choices: build
cmd
exec
push
explanation: ACR Tasks YAML defines three step types: build, push, and cmd; the cmd step runs an arbitrary container command, which is used to run and test a container. build builds an image and push pushes it; neither runs an arbitrary test command. exec is not a valid ACR Tasks step type.

stem: Wide World Importers geo-replicates a Premium registry across four regions and is surprised by the storage bill. A 2 GiB image is pushed once. How is storage billed, and how do API rate limits behave across the geo-replicas?
choices: Storage is billed per geo-replica, so 2 GiB replicated to four replicas is charged as 8 GiB; API rate limits are per-replica
Storage is billed per geo-replica but API rate limits are shared across all replicas
Storage is billed once and API rate limits are per-replica
Storage is billed once because replicas share the tier storage limit; API rate limits are per-registry
explanation: Storage is billed per geo-replica (2 GiB times four replicas equals 8 GiB), and API throttling limits are geo-replica-specific. Although the tier storage limit is shared for quota purposes, billing is per replica. API rate limits are per-replica, not per-registry, which is why spreading traffic across regional endpoints helps.

stem: Relecloud must import a public image into a registry, then block its use until CVE scanning, SBOM evaluation, and image signing complete. The workload team has different risk tolerances across projects and wants to decide promotion themselves. Which Quarantine pattern variant fits best?
choices: Keep the image in the quarantine registry, publish validation results via an API, and let each workload team pull only if results meet its risk tolerance
Skip the quarantine registry and scan the image directly in the trusted registry after promotion
Have the orchestrator always auto-promote passing images to the trusted registry and delete the quarantine copy
Grant every workload team AcrQuarantineWriter so each can push directly to production
explanation: The pull variant keeps the image in quarantine, exposes validation results through an API, and lets each team decide based on its own risk tolerance, which suits multiple teams with differing tolerances. Auto-promotion removes the per-team decision the scenario requires. Scanning after promotion defeats the purpose of quarantine isolation. AcrQuarantineWriter governs quarantine status, not direct production push, and does not implement per-team promotion.

stem: Contoso pins its West Europe AKS cluster to myregistry.westeurope.geo.azurecr.io in the deployment manifest and enables dedicated data endpoints. When pods pull image layers, to which host does the 307 redirect point?
choices: myregistry.azurecr.io, because layer downloads always route through the global endpoint
myregistry.westeurope.data.azurecr.io, because the layer redirect always stays within the same region as the regional endpoint
myregistry.eastus.data.azurecr.io, because layer downloads always route to the home region data endpoint
A blob.core.windows.net storage account in the home region, regardless of dedicated data endpoints
explanation: With dedicated data endpoints enabled, a pull from a regional geo endpoint redirects layer blob downloads to the same-region dedicated data endpoint, never cross-region. Layer downloads from a regional endpoint do not route through the global endpoint. With dedicated data endpoints enabled, layers redirect to the data endpoint, not a raw storage account URL. The redirect is same-region, never to the home region's data endpoint by default.

stem:
Woodgrove creates a Docker Hub artifact cache rule in a Premium registry. Complete the command so the rule references an existing Key Vault-backed credential set for the authenticated Docker Hub upstream.

```
az acr cache create -r WoodgroveReg -n UbuntuRule \
  -s docker.io/library/ubuntu -t ubuntu ________ DockerHubCredSet
```
choices: -c
--identity
--sync-token
--scope-map
explanation: The -c parameter attaches an existing credential set to a cache rule, which Docker Hub requires because it supports authenticated pulls only. --identity is used for ACR-to-ACR caching with a managed identity, not a Key Vault credential set. --scope-map applies to non-Entra tokens. --sync-token is a connected registry parameter, not an artifact cache one.

stem:
Fabrikam migrates a registry to support Microsoft Entra ABAC conditions on role assignments while keeping standard RBAC assignments. Complete the command that sets the role assignment mode.

```
az acr update --name FabrikamReg \
  --role-assignment-mode ________
```
choices: rbac-abac
abac-only
rbac-registry
entra-conditions
explanation: Specifying rbac-abac retains standard Entra RBAC assignments while optionally applying ABAC conditions for repository-level access control. abac-only, rbac-registry, and entra-conditions are not valid values for --role-assignment-mode; rbac-abac is the mode that enables ABAC repository permissions.

stem:
Alpine Ski House configures an App Service custom container so App Service forwards HTTP requests to the container's listening port of 8000. Complete the app setting name.

```
az webapp config appsettings set --resource-group rg-alpine \
  --name alpine-app --settings ________=8000
```
choices: WEBSITES_CONTAINER_PORT
WEBSITE_PORT
HTTP_PLATFORM_PORT
WEBSITES_PORT
explanation: WEBSITES_PORT tells App Service which container port to forward HTTP requests to when it is not the default port 80. WEBSITE_PORT, WEBSITES_CONTAINER_PORT, and HTTP_PLATFORM_PORT are not the recognized app setting; WEBSITES_PORT is the correct name.

stem:
Trey Research configures an App Service web app to pull its container image from Azure Container Registry using its managed identity. Complete the generic configuration property that turns on managed-identity credentials for the ACR pull.

```
az webapp config set --resource-group rg-trey --name trey-app \
  --generic-configurations '{"________": true}'
```
choices: useAcrManagedIdentity
acrManagedIdentityEnabled
acrUseManagedIdentityCreds
acrIdentityPullEnabled
explanation: Setting acrUseManagedIdentityCreds to true configures the app to pull from Azure Container Registry using its managed identity. useAcrManagedIdentity, acrManagedIdentityEnabled, and acrIdentityPullEnabled are not the property name; acrUseManagedIdentityCreds is correct.

stem:
Relecloud creates a connected registry resource whose clients should only be able to pull artifacts, which is also the secure-by-default mode. Complete the mode value.

```
az acr connected-registry create --registry RelecloudReg \
  --name edge-ro --parent edge-rw --repository "hello-world" \
  --mode ________
```
choices: Pull
ReadWrite
Mirror
ReadOnly
explanation: ReadOnly is the default connected registry mode and allows clients to pull (read) artifacts only. ReadWrite allows push and pull. Mirror and Registry are other valid modes but do not restrict clients to pull-only in the secure-by-default sense; Pull is not a valid mode value.

stem: Contoso converts a registry from RBAC-only mode to RBAC Registry + ABAC Repository Permissions and must preserve access for an identity that currently holds AcrPull. Which two role assignments together provide equivalent registry-wide read and catalog-list access after the switch? (Select two.)
choices: Container Registry Repository Catalog Lister
The legacy AcrPull role reassigned in the ABAC-enabled registry
Container Registry Repository Reader assigned without ABAC conditions
Container Registry Repository Contributor scoped to all repositories
Container Registry Contributor and Data Access Configuration Administrator
explanation: The AcrPull equivalent in an ABAC-enabled registry is Container Registry Repository Reader (assigned without conditions for registry-wide read) plus Container Registry Repository Catalog Lister for catalog listing. Repository Contributor grants delete permissions beyond AcrPull's read scope. Legacy AcrPull is not honored in ABAC-enabled registries. The Contributor and Data Access Configuration Administrator role is a control plane role granting az acr login and configuration, not data plane pull.

stem: Best For You Organics performs a slot swap between a staging slot and the production slot in App Service. Which two configuration elements are swapped (follow the content) rather than staying with the slot? (Select two.)
choices: Scale settings
Custom domain names
Managed identities
App settings not marked as deployment slot settings
Language framework settings such as .NET version
explanation: Language framework settings swap with the content, and app settings swap unless they are marked as sticky deployment slot settings. Custom domain names, managed identities, and scale settings are slot-specific and are not swapped.

stem: Munson's Pickles hardens a Premium registry. Which two statements about ACR geo-replication during a home region outage are correct? (Select two.)
choices: ACR Tasks continue to run because they fail over to a healthy region
Image push, pull, and delete continue to work through the remaining geo-replicas
Registry configuration changes such as network rules can still be modified
Regional endpoints for the failed home region remain available
Authentication with managed identities, service principals, and repository-scoped tokens continues to function
explanation: During a home region outage only the control plane is affected; data plane operations (push, pull, delete) continue through remaining geo-replicas, and all authentication methods keep working. Registry configuration changes require the home region control plane and are unavailable during the outage. ACR Tasks are bound to the home region and do not run. The home region's own regional endpoint is unavailable while that region is down.

stem: Fourth Coffee designs an ACR Tasks multi-step YAML workflow. Which two are valid top-level constructs of an acr-task.yaml file? (Select two.)
choices: Task properties such as version, stepTimeout, and workingDirectory
A slots array defining staging and production task targets
A triggers block listing base-image, commit, and schedule as YAML step types
A sitecontainers block declaring the main and sidecar images
Task step types build, push, and cmd
explanation: An acr-task.yaml file is composed of task properties (like version, stepTimeout, workingDirectory), step types (build, push, cmd), and step properties. Triggers such as base-image, commit, and schedule are configured on the task, not as YAML step types. slots and sitecontainers are App Service constructs, not ACR Tasks YAML constructs.

stem: Fabrikam converts a KEDA ScaledObject that triggers on Azure Service Bus queue depth into an Azure Container Apps custom scale rule. The app must scale to zero when idle and authenticate to Service Bus without storing any secret. Which single value from the KEDA scaler specification must be supplied as the Container Apps --scale-rule-type parameter?
choices: The scaler trigger's type value, such as azure-servicebus
The metadata queueName value
The TriggerAuthentication authenticationRef name
The messageCount threshold value
explanation: When you map a KEDA ScaledObject to a Container Apps custom rule, the trigger's type value (for example azure-servicebus) becomes the --scale-rule-type, and the metadata becomes --scale-rule-metadata. queueName and messageCount belong under --scale-rule-metadata, not the rule type. authenticationRef points to a TriggerAuthentication object that maps to scale-rule auth entries or managed identity, not to the rule type.

stem: Woodgrove deploys a Container App with ingress disabled because it only runs a background worker. The team defines neither a minReplicas value nor a custom scale rule. After deployment the worker never starts processing. What is the root cause?
choices: Ingress must be enabled for any Container App to run
Background workers are not supported on Container Apps
With no ingress, no minReplicas, and no scale rule, the app scales to zero and has no trigger to start
The default HTTP scale rule requires TCP ingress to function
explanation: If ingress is disabled and you define neither minReplicas of one or more nor a custom scale rule, the app scales to zero with no way to start back up. Ingress is optional for background workers. Container Apps fully supports non-HTTP workers. The default HTTP rule is irrelevant here because ingress is disabled, which is exactly why a custom rule or a minimum replica count is needed.

stem: Relecloud enables Dapr on two container apps: an order publisher and an inventory subscriber. Both must exchange messages over the same Dapr pub/sub topic and be discoverable by a stable identity. Which Dapr setting simultaneously serves service discovery, state encapsulation, and the pub/sub consumer ID for each app?
choices: --dapr-app-id
--dapr-app-port
--dapr-app-protocol
--dapr-max-request-size
explanation: The Dapr app ID is a unique identifier used for service discovery, state encapsulation, and as the pub/sub consumer ID. app-port tells Dapr which port your app listens on. app-protocol selects http or grpc. max-request-size sets the maximum request body size. None of these serve as the app identity or consumer ID.

stem: Litware configures a Dapr state store component in a Container Apps environment so a Node.js app can persist orders in Azure Blob Storage using managed identity. The component YAML must declare the correct component type. Which componentType value is required for an Azure Blob Storage state store?
choices: pubsub.azure.servicebus.topics
state.azure.blobstorage
bindings.azure.blobstorage
secretstores.azure.keyvault
explanation: An Azure Blob Storage state store uses the component type state.azure.blobstorage. pubsub.azure.servicebus.topics is a publish and subscribe broker. bindings.azure.blobstorage is an output binding, not a state store. secretstores.azure.keyvault is a secret store. Only the state.* prefix defines a state management component.

stem: Proseware changes the Dapr sidecar app protocol on a container app that runs in multiple-revision mode, expecting a new revision to be created for rollback. Instead, no new revision appears and every existing revision restarts. Why does this happen?
choices: Multiple-revision mode disables all revision creation
Dapr is not supported in multiple-revision mode
Dapr configurations are application-scope changes, so they restart existing revisions rather than create a new one
The change failed silently and was never applied
explanation: Dapr configurations in Container Apps are application-scope changes. In multiple-revision mode they do not create a new revision; instead all existing revisions restart with the updated values. Multiple-revision mode still creates revisions for template changes. Dapr is supported in multiple-revision mode. The restart behavior confirms the change was applied, not that it failed silently.

stem: Coho Vineyard has two container apps in one environment. App A must call App B, the call must stay inside the environment and never traverse the public internet, and traffic between them must be TLS encrypted without App B exposing a public endpoint. Which combination meets all three requirements?
choices: Set App B ingress external to true and require a client certificate
Disable ingress on App B and enable session affinity
Set App B ingress to TCP transport with allowInsecure true
Set App B ingress external to false and enable environment peer-to-peer encryption
explanation: Internal ingress (external set to false) keeps App B reachable only within the environment, and environment peer-to-peer encryption TLS-encrypts traffic between apps using a managed private certificate. External true exposes App B publicly. Disabling ingress removes the endpoint App A needs to call. allowInsecure true permits unencrypted traffic, defeating the encryption requirement.

stem: Alpine Ski House runs a stateful Container App whose users must keep hitting the same replica across requests. The app uses HTTP ingress. After enabling sticky sessions, requests still spread across replicas. Which requirement was most likely violated?
choices: Session affinity requires TCP ingress rather than HTTP
Session affinity requires peer-to-peer encryption enabled
Session affinity requires a minimum of three replicas
Session affinity requires the app to run in single revision mode
explanation: Session affinity is only supported when the app is in single revision mode with HTTP ingress; stickiness is enforced with an HTTP cookie. Session affinity requires HTTP, not TCP, ingress. It does not depend on peer-to-peer encryption or on any minimum replica count. Running in multiple-revision mode would break the affinity guarantee.

stem: Munson's Pickles needs a sidecar container to process log files that the main app container writes. The two containers run in the same replica and must share a temporary volume that survives a single container restart but need not persist beyond the replica. Which Container Apps storage type fits?
choices: Container-scoped ephemeral storage
An Azure Files permanent volume
Replica-scoped EmptyDir ephemeral storage
An Azure NetApp Files volume
explanation: Replica-scoped storage is an EmptyDir volume shared by all containers in the same replica; files persist for the lifetime of the replica, including across a single container restart. Container-scoped storage is visible only to one container and disappears on that container's restart. Azure Files is permanent shared storage, more than required and not scoped to the replica. Azure NetApp Files is not supported for Container Apps mounts.

stem: Southridge Video wants a Container App to write output files to a share that other external systems can read, and the data must survive replica restarts. The team plans to mount Azure Blob Storage or Azure NetApp Files directly. Which statement is correct about the supported choice?
choices: Azure Blob Storage can be mounted directly as a Container Apps volume
Azure NetApp Files can be mounted directly as a Container Apps volume
Azure Files is the supported permanent volume; Blob Storage and NetApp Files mounts are not supported
Only replica-scoped EmptyDir volumes persist data across replicas
explanation: Azure Container Apps supports Azure Files for permanent storage. Mounting file shares from Azure NetApp Files or Azure Blob Storage is not supported. Neither Blob Storage nor NetApp Files can be mounted as a Container Apps volume. EmptyDir is replica-scoped ephemeral storage that does not persist beyond the replica, so it cannot make data durable for external systems.

stem: Nod Publishers wants a production revision and a staging revision of the same container app, each reachable at its own stable URL, with no risk that a new deployment silently reroutes production traffic. Which Container Apps feature provides a persistent per-revision URL that you can move deliberately between revisions?
choices: Session affinity cookies
Ephemeral storage mounts
Revision labels
Dapr service invocation
explanation: Revision labels provide a unique, stable URL for a revision. A label can be moved between revisions to reroute its traffic deliberately, and each revision can hold at most one label. Session affinity pins a client to a replica, not a revision URL. Ephemeral storage is unrelated to routing. Dapr service invocation handles internal service-to-service calls, not external labeled endpoints.

stem: VanArsdel runs a container app in multiple-revision mode and wants to send 80 percent of traffic to a known-good revision and 20 percent to a new revision for canary testing. Which condition must the traffic-splitting configuration satisfy?
choices: Each revision must run in its own environment
Session affinity must be enabled first
The app must use TCP ingress
The combined weight of all traffic rules must equal 100
explanation: Traffic splitting is weight based, and the combined weight of all traffic split rules must equal 100 percent. Revisions can be targeted by name or by label. Revisions in a split share one environment and one app. Session affinity is not a prerequisite and only applies in single revision mode. Traffic splitting works with HTTP ingress, not a TCP-only requirement.

stem: Trey Research needs a Container Apps job that runs one execution for each message arriving in an Azure Service Bus queue and then stops, with several messages processed in parallel. Which job trigger type and scaling concept apply?
choices: Event trigger type using a KEDA-based scaling rule
Manual trigger type with an HTTP scale rule
Schedule trigger type with a cron expression
Manual trigger type with session affinity
explanation: Event-driven jobs use the Event trigger type and are started by supported KEDA custom scalers such as a Service Bus queue scaler; each execution typically processes one event. Manual jobs start on demand only. Scheduled jobs run on a cron timetable, not per message. HTTP scale rules and session affinity apply to apps, not to event-driven job execution counts.

stem: Blue Yonder defines an event-driven Container Apps job. Each triggered batch must run up to four executions concurrently, and the job is considered complete only after three of those executions succeed. Which two eventTriggerConfig properties express these constraints, and what is their required relationship?
choices: replicaTimeout 4 and replicaRetryLimit 3, where retry must exceed timeout
parallelism 4 and replicaCompletionCount 3, where replicaCompletionCount must be equal to or less than parallelism
minReplicas 4 and maxReplicas 3, where max must exceed min
parallelism 3 and replicaCompletionCount 4, where completion must exceed parallelism
explanation: parallelism sets how many replicas run at once, and replicaCompletionCount sets the minimum successful completions before the job finishes; replicaCompletionCount must be equal to or less than parallelism. replicaTimeout and replicaRetryLimit govern per-replica runtime and retries, not concurrency and completion counts. minReplicas and maxReplicas are app scaling terms, not job completion terms. Completion count cannot exceed parallelism.

stem: Consolidated Messenger needs a Container Apps job that generates a financial report every night at midnight without any external event source. Which job trigger type and configuration are correct?
choices: Schedule trigger type with a cron expression such as 0 0 * * *
Event trigger type with a queue scale rule
Manual trigger type invoked by Azure Resource Manager
Schedule trigger type with a KEDA ScaledObject
explanation: A recurring time-based job uses the Schedule trigger type configured with a cron expression, for example 0 0 * * * for midnight. Event jobs require an event source such as a queue. Manual jobs require an explicit on-demand start each time. Scheduled jobs use a cron expression, not a KEDA ScaledObject, which applies to event-driven scaling.

stem: Fourth Coffee configures health probes for a Container App. The team wants an exec command probe and a gRPC liveness check like they used on raw Kubernetes. Which statement about Container Apps probe support is correct?
choices: Container Apps supports exec and gRPC probes identically to Kubernetes
Container Apps supports only TCP or HTTP(S) probes; exec and gRPC are not supported
Container Apps supports gRPC probes but not HTTP probes
Container Apps supports named ports for probes but not integer ports
explanation: Container Apps health probes support only TCP or HTTP(S). exec probes and gRPC are not supported, and named ports are not supported (ports must be integers). exec and gRPC probes are explicitly unsupported. HTTP probes are supported. Ports must be integers, so named ports are not supported, making the remaining options incorrect.

stem: Graphic Design Institute has a Java Container App that takes a long time to initialize. During rollout the platform keeps marking the revision unhealthy and restarting the container before the app finishes starting. Which probe adjustment most directly resolves premature restarts for a slow-starting app?
choices: Lower the liveness probe periodSeconds to 1
Increase the startup and liveness probe initial delay so the app has time to start
Disable the readiness probe entirely
Set the readiness probe failureThreshold to 1
explanation: For apps with extended startup time, increasing the initial delay (and startup or liveness thresholds) gives the app enough time to start before probes can trigger a restart. Lowering periodSeconds probes more aggressively and worsens premature restarts. Disabling the readiness probe risks routing traffic to a not-ready replica. Setting readiness failureThreshold to 1 makes the check less tolerant, increasing false unhealthy states.

stem: Adventure Works dedicates an AKS node pool to GPU workloads and must ensure that pods already running on those nodes without a matching toleration are evicted immediately when the taint is applied. Which taint effect achieves immediate eviction of non-tolerating pods?
choices: NoSchedule
PreferNoSchedule
PreferNoExecute
NoExecute
explanation: NoExecute immediately evicts pods already running on the node if they do not have a matching toleration; a matching toleration can keep them, optionally bounded by tolerationSeconds. NoSchedule blocks new non-tolerating pods but does not evict existing ones. PreferNoSchedule is a soft preference only. PreferNoExecute is not a valid taint effect.

stem: Wingtip Toys adds an Azure Spot node pool to an AKS cluster to run interruptible batch jobs cheaply. The team wants only batch pods to land on Spot nodes and needs those pods to schedule there successfully. Which pod-side configuration is required?
choices: Only a nodeSelector for the region label
A toleration for kubernetes.azure.com/scalesetpriority=spot:NoSchedule plus node affinity for the spot label
A privileged securityContext
A PodDisruptionBudget with maxUnavailable zero
explanation: A Spot node pool carries the taint kubernetes.azure.com/scalesetpriority=spot:NoSchedule and the label kubernetes.azure.com/scalesetpriority=spot, so pods need a matching toleration and node affinity to be scheduled there. A region nodeSelector does not tolerate the spot taint. A privileged securityContext is unrelated to scheduling. A PodDisruptionBudget governs voluntary disruptions, not initial scheduling onto tainted spot nodes.

stem: Lamna Healthcare tries to make a Spot node pool the cluster's default (system) node pool and later change its SpotMaxPrice. Both operations fail. Which pair of Spot node pool constraints explains the failures?
choices: A Spot pool can be default, but SpotMaxPrice is immutable
A Spot pool cannot use Virtual Machine Scale Sets, and SpotMaxPrice must be zero
A Spot pool cannot be the default node pool, and ScaleSetPriority and SpotMaxPrice cannot be changed after creation
A Spot pool must be default, and SpotMaxPrice can only decrease
explanation: A Spot node pool can only be a secondary pool, not the default. You cannot change ScaleSetPriority or SpotMaxPrice after creation. A Spot pool cannot be the default pool. Spot pools must use Virtual Machine Scale Sets, not avoid them. SpotMaxPrice must be minus one or a positive value with up to five decimals, and it is immutable, so it cannot simply decrease.

stem: Margie's Travel must scale an AKS workload on the number of messages in an Azure Service Bus queue, not on CPU or memory. A teammate proposes attaching both a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler and a KEDA ScaledObject to the same Deployment. Which statement is correct?
choices: HPA scales on event counts, so KEDA is redundant
KEDA is event-driven and uses HPA internally; combining a separate HPA with a ScaledObject on the same workload causes conflicting scaling
KEDA cannot scale on Azure Service Bus queues
HPA and KEDA must both be attached for queue scaling to work
explanation: HPA is metrics-driven (CPU and memory), while KEDA is event-driven and creates an HPA in the background. Combining a manual HPA with a KEDA ScaledObject on the same workload makes them compete, causing odd scaling. HPA scales on resource metrics, not event counts. KEDA supports the Azure Service Bus scaler. Only the KEDA ScaledObject is needed for queue scaling; adding a separate HPA is the source of the conflict.

stem: School of Fine Art enables the AKS KEDA add-on and then tries to install a second external metrics adapter for a custom scaler. The custom adapter fails to function. Which KEDA add-on limitation explains this?
choices: KEDA requires the cluster autoscaler to be disabled
KEDA cannot coexist with any Deployment
KEDA disables the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler API
Only one external metrics server is allowed in the cluster, so the KEDA add-on must be the only external metrics adapter
explanation: Due to an upstream limitation, only one external metric server can run in a Kubernetes cluster, so the KEDA add-on must be the only installed external metrics adapter. KEDA works alongside the cluster autoscaler. KEDA scales Deployments rather than blocking them. KEDA relies on the HPA API internally rather than disabling it.

stem: Woodgrove updates an AKS Deployment and wants the rollout to bring up extra pods above the desired count so new pods become ready before old ones are terminated, minimizing downtime. Which Deployment rolling-update field controls the extra pods created during the update?
choices: maxUnavailable
minReadySeconds
maxSurge
progressDeadlineSeconds
explanation: maxSurge specifies the maximum number of pods that can be created beyond the desired count during a rolling update, letting new pods become ready before old ones are removed. maxUnavailable limits how many pods can be unavailable, not how many extra are created. minReadySeconds delays marking a pod available. progressDeadlineSeconds bounds how long a rollout may stall before it is considered failed.

stem: Contoso upgrades an AKS node pool in a region with tight quota, so surging extra nodes is not possible. The team must upgrade using existing capacity even though it accepts brief workload disruption. Which node-pool upgrade setting performs an in-place upgrade by cordoning and draining existing nodes without adding surge nodes?
choices: --max-unavailable
--max-surge
--node-osdisk-size
--node-count
explanation: max unavailable does not create surge nodes; AKS cordons and drains the specified number of existing nodes at a time, enabling an in-place upgrade when surge capacity is unavailable. max surge requires additional node capacity, which is exactly what is unavailable. node-osdisk-size sets disk size, and node-count changes pool size; neither controls upgrade unavailability behavior.

stem: Litware sees an AKS container repeatedly terminated and restarted while the rest of its pod keeps running. kubectl describe pod shows reason OOMKilled and exit code 137. Which interpretation is correct?
choices: The whole pod was evicted by the kubelet for node memory pressure
A single container exceeded its memory limit and was terminated by the Linux OOM killer, then restarted
